newsitem.title: CHINA: Britain's LSE looks for first China listing soon.
newsitem.headline: Britain's LSE looks for first China listing soon.

text.p: A major Chinese company could list on the London Stock Exchange before the end of 1996, after China and Britain on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to clear the procedural way, British officials said.

"The Memorandum... will allow Chinese companies to list their securities on the London Stock Exchange," said British Treasury Economic Secretary Angela Knight before signing the MOU in Beijing's cavernous Great Hall of the People.
"I look forward with expectation to the first listing on the London Stock Exchange of a major Chinese company shortly, and I trust there will be many more," Knight said.

Officials of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) said the first listing could take place before the end of the year, but declined to name the most likely candidate from among China's many capital-starved enterprises.
The LSE's advisers were working hard to attract Chinese firms to list in London, said deputy chairman Ian Salter.

"We are encouraged by what we have heard that there will be a listing fairly soon," Salter told reporters. "This is the first memorandum of understanding (China has) done with anyone in Europe. It's very promising."
Datang Power, which is expected to seek listing in Hong Kong in the next few months, was one company being considered for London listing, industry sources said.
Some 82 Chinese companies have already issued foreign currency shares in China for overseas investors. Others are listed in Hong Kong, with a further handful traded in New York.

The 24 companies listed overseas had already raised $4.4 billion, and China would inevitably make further progress into international capital markets, said China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) chairman Zhou Daojiong.

China has already signed MOUs with exchanges in Singapore and Australia, and CSRC officials have said diplomatic disputes over the return to China of the British colony of Hong Kong caused the Sino-British agreement to be long delayed.
Hong Kong, which returns to Beijing rule on July 1, 1997, has for years been a source of friction between Beijing and London, but both sides say ties have warmed in recent months.

The London exchange would be a complementary addition to Hong Kong for Chinese companies, with some taking primary listings in Hong Kong and secondary listings in London while others might do the reverse, Salter said but gave no details.

The LSE's advisers were being very careful to ensure that Chinese firms, which have often performed poorly on the Hong Kong and New York exchanges, passed muster for London listings, exchange officials said.

Chinese listed companies have in the past drawn fire from foreign and domestic investors for non-standard accounting practices and for failing to live up to the investment plans outlined in their prospectuses.
